title: Κῦμα θαλάσσης
titleEn: Diomedes Rebuked and the Armies Clash — Iliad 4.364–456
part: Diomedes Rebuked and the Armies Clash (4.364–456)
source: Homer, The Iliad, Greek text of D. B. Monro and T. W. Allen, Homeri Opera, tomi I–II, 3rd ed. (Oxford Classical Texts; Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1920), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-greekLit tlg0012.tlg001.perseus-grc2, sha256 ae8b617018c6e5af. Text as printed: the edition sets no quotation marks round speeches, and none are added. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca — an admitted convention; Homer's own pronunciation was older and is not recoverable in detail. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; ï for a separately sounded ι; accents omitted). Scansion: made by program from the text and checked; it shows one defensible reading of each line, and the notes say where a line is irregular. All translations were made fresh from the Greek for Lectorium.
about: Agamemnon, still going along the ranks, finds Diomedes standing among his horses and chariot with Sthenelus beside him, and reviles him for holding back. He tells how Diomedes' father Tydeus once went as an envoy to the Cadmeans, challenged them to contests and beat them all with Athena's help, then killed fifty men who lay in ambush for him and let only Maeon go home; the son, he says, is the worse fighter. Diomedes says nothing, out of respect for the king, but Sthenelus answers that they are better than their fathers, since they took seven-gated Thebes with fewer men. Diomedes tells him to be quiet: Agamemnon will have the glory if the Achaeans win and the grief if they are cut down, so the two of them should think of fighting. He leaps from his chariot with a terrible clang of bronze. The Danaan lines then move forward like a wave coming in from the sea, silent under their leaders, while the Trojans, called from many lands, are loud as ewes bleating for their lambs. Ares, Athena, Dread, Terror and Strife rouse the two armies, and they crash together like two torrents meeting in a ravine.

sentences.t: ὣς εἰπὼν τοὺς μὲν λίπεν αὐτοῦ, βῆ δὲ μετ’ ἄλλους.
sentences.tr: hōs eipōn tous men lipen autou, bē de met’ allous.
sentences.l: So having spoken, those he left on the spot, and went among others;
sentences.i: So he spoke, and left them there, and went on to others;
sentences.n: ὣς εἰπών ‘so having spoken’ closes Agamemnon’s speech to Odysseus. τοὺς μέν ‘those’ (Odysseus, Menestheus and their men) is set against ἄλλους ‘others’, to whom he now goes: μετά with the accusative means ‘among, to join’. λίπεν and βῆ are aorists without the augment (ἔλιπεν, ἔβη), and αὐτοῦ is the adverb ‘on the spot, there’. The line is the same as 4.292, and the English is kept. A new paragraph begins at 364.

sentences.t:
εὗρε δὲ Τυδέος υἱὸν ὑπέρθυμον Διομήδεα
ἑσταότ’ ἔν θ’ ἵπποισι καὶ ἅρμασι κολλητοῖσι·
sentences.tr:
heure de Tydeos huion hyperthymon Diomēdea
hestaot’ en th’ hippoisi kai harmasi kollētoisi·
sentences.l:
And he found the son of Tydeus, high-spirited Diomedes,
standing among horses and well-joined chariots;
sentences.i: And he found the son of Tydeus, high-spirited Diomedes, standing amid horses and well-joined chariots;
sentences.n: εὗρε is the aorist of εὑρίσκω without the augment. Τυδέος υἱόν ‘the son of Tydeus’ is a periphrasis that the line then spells out with the name Διομήδεα (the epic accusative); ὑπέρθυμον ‘high-spirited’ is a stock epithet. ἑσταότ’ is the elided perfect participle of ἵστημι ‘stand’ (accusative, agreeing with the son), and ἔν θ’ is ἐν τε, the τε answering καί in ‘both among horses and chariots’. ἵπποισι and κολλητοῖσι have the epic dative plural in -οισι, while ἅρμασι is the ordinary dative plural of ἅρμα; the plural ἅρματα can mean one chariot, and κολλητός ‘well-joined’ is literally ‘glued together’, of the fitted joints.

sentences.t: πὰρ δέ οἱ ἑστήκει Σθένελος Καπανήϊος υἱός.
sentences.tr: par de hoi hestēkei Sthenelos Kapanēïos huios.
sentences.l: and beside him was standing Sthenelus, the Capaneian son.
sentences.i: and beside him stood Sthenelus, the son of Capaneus.
sentences.n: πὰρ is παρά with its last vowel cut off, and οἱ is the dative ‘him’, not the article. ἑστήκει is the pluperfect of ἵστημι: past in sense (‘was standing’), perfect in form. Καπανήϊος is an adjective, ‘of Capaneus’, used where English has a genitive; Sthenelus is Diomedes’ companion, and he is the one who answers the king at 404.

sentences.t:
καὶ τὸν μὲν νείκεσσεν ἰδὼν κρείων Ἀγαμέμνων,
καί μιν φωνήσας ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα·
sentences.tr:
kai ton men neikessen idōn kreiōn Agamemnōn,
kai min phōnēsas epea pteroenta prosēuda·
sentences.l:
And him indeed reviled, seeing him, lord Agamemnon,
and, lifting his voice, to him winged words he spoke:
sentences.i: Lord Agamemnon saw him and reviled him, and lifting his voice he spoke winged words to him:
sentences.n: καὶ τὸν μέν ‘and him on his side’ waits for its contrast at 401, τὸν δ’ οὔ τι προσέφη, where Diomedes answers nothing. νείκεσσεν is the aorist of νεικέω ‘revile’, with the doubled σ of the epic form, and ἰδών ‘seeing’ gives the occasion. κρείων ‘lord’ is the stock word beside Agamemnon’s name. Line 369 is the formula that stands at 1.201 and 2.7; here μιν is masculine, Diomedes, so the English says ‘to him’ where 1.201 said ‘to her’. The edition prints no quotation marks: the speech begins with the next line.

sentences.t:
ὤ μοι Τυδέος υἱὲ δαΐφρονος ἱπποδάμοιο
τί πτώσσεις, τί δ’ ὀπιπεύεις πολέμοιο γεφύρας;
sentences.tr:
ō moi Tydeos huie daïphronos hippodamoio
ti ptōsseis, ti d’ opipeueis polemoio gephyras;
sentences.l:
“Oh me, son of Tydeus, wise-minded, horse-taming,
why do you cower, why do you peer about at the bridges of war?
sentences.i: “Oh me, son of wise-hearted Tydeus, tamer of horses, why do you cower, and why do you peer about at the bridges of war?
sentences.n: ὤ μοι is a cry of dismay, here opening a rebuke. Τυδέος υἱέ is the vocative ‘son of Tydeus’, and the two genitives δαΐφρονος ἱπποδάμοιο belong to Tydeus, not to his son: ἱππόδαμος ‘horse-taming’ is a stock epithet, and δαΐφρων is rendered ‘wise-minded’, though it may instead mean ‘warlike’ (the ancients were not sure). πτώσσεις ‘you cower’ and ὀπιπεύεις ‘you peer about’ are presents. πολέμοιο γεφύρας ‘the bridges of war’ is a figure the Greek does not explain; it is usually taken to mean the open ground between the two armies, which men have to cross, but the word itself is just ‘bridges’.

sentences.t:
οὐ μὲν Τυδέϊ γ’ ὧδε φίλον πτωσκαζέμεν ἦεν,
ἀλλὰ πολὺ πρὸ φίλων ἑτάρων δηΐοισι μάχεσθαι,
ὡς φάσαν οἵ μιν ἴδοντο πονεύμενον·
sentences.tr:
ou men Tydeï g’ hōde philon ptōskazemen ēen,
alla poly pro philōn hetarōn dēïoisi machesthai,
hōs phasan hoi min idonto poneumenon·
sentences.i: Tydeus did not like to cower in this way, but to fight the enemy far in front of his dear companions, as they said who saw him toiling;
sentences.n: οὐ μὲν … γε ‘not indeed’ is emphatic. φίλον ‘dear, pleasing’ has to be supplied again before μάχεσθαι in the second line (‘but dear to fight’). πτωσκαζέμεν is an infinitive in -έμεν (= πτωσκάζειν), a form of πτώσσω ‘cower’ with the -σκ- of repeated action, so ‘keep cowering’; ἦεν = ἦν. δηΐοισι is the dative plural of δήϊος ‘hostile’ used as a noun, ‘the enemy’. φάσαν = ἔφασαν (no augment) ‘they said’, and ἴδοντο is an aorist middle of ὁράω ‘saw’, also without augment; πονεύμενον is πονεόμενον, the participle of πονέομαι ‘toil’.

sentences.t:
οὐ γὰρ ἔγωγε
ἤντησ’ οὐδὲ ἴδον·
sentences.tr:
ou gar egōge
ēntēs’ oude idon·
sentences.l:
for I myself
neither met him nor saw him;
sentences.i: for I myself never met him or saw him;
sentences.n: οὐ γὰρ ἔγωγε ‘for I myself … not’ gives the reason why Agamemnon reports what others said: ἔγωγε is ἐγώ with the strengthening -γε. ἤντησ’ is the elided aorist ἤντησα of ἀντάω ‘meet’, and ἴδον is an aorist without the augment (= εἶδον ‘saw’). The object ‘him’ is not expressed. The half-line also stands at Odyssey 4.200.

sentences.t: περὶ δ’ ἄλλων φασὶ γενέσθαι.
sentences.tr: peri d’ allōn phasi genesthai.
sentences.l: and beyond others, they say, to have been superior.
sentences.i: and they say that he surpassed the rest.
sentences.n: περί … γενέσθαι is tmesis, the preverb standing apart from its verb: περιγενέσθαι ‘surpass, be superior to’, with the genitive ἄλλων ‘than others’. The infinitive depends on φασί ‘they say’ (the present of φημί), and its subject, Tydeus, is left understood. The line also stands at Odyssey 4.201.

sentences.t:
ἤτοι μὲν γὰρ ἄτερ πολέμου εἰσῆλθε Μυκήνας
ξεῖνος ἅμ’ ἀντιθέῳ Πολυνείκεϊ λαὸν ἀγείρων·
sentences.tr:
ētoi men gar ater polemou eisēlthe Mykēnas
xeinos ham’ antitheōi Polyneikeï laon ageirōn·
sentences.l:
For truly, without war, he came into Mycenae,
a stranger, together with godlike Polynices, gathering a people;
sentences.i: For he came into Mycenae without war, as a stranger, together with godlike Polynices, gathering troops;
sentences.n: ἤτοι is printed as one word in this edition; with μὲν γάρ it gives the ground for what has just been said: ‘for in fact’. ἄτερ ‘without’ takes the genitive, εἰσῆλθε is the aorist of εἰσέρχομαι ‘go into’, and Μυκήνας is the plural accusative of the city’s name. ξεῖνος is ‘stranger, guest’, a man from abroad who is received as a guest. ἀντιθέῳ ‘godlike’ is a stock epithet, and Πολυνείκεϊ is the epic dative of Πολυνείκης. Agamemnon is telling the story of the Argive attack on Thebes, which Tydeus and Polynices first prepared by seeking allies at Mycenae.

sentences.t:
οἳ δὲ τότ’ ἐστρατόωνθ’ ἱερὰ πρὸς τείχεα Θήβης,
καί ῥα μάλα λίσσοντο δόμεν κλειτοὺς ἐπικούρους·
sentences.tr:
hoi de tot’ estratoōnth’ hiera pros teichea Thēbēs,
kai rha mala lissonto domen kleitous epikourous·
sentences.l:
And they at that time were encamped against the sacred walls of Thebes,
and so very much begged them to give famous allies;
sentences.i: They were then encamped against the sacred walls of Thebes, and they begged them earnestly to give them famous allies;
sentences.n: οἳ δέ ‘and they’ uses the relative form as a pronoun; those meant are the Argives before Thebes, not the Mycenaeans of the line before. ἐστρατόωνθ’ is the imperfect of στρατάομαι ‘be encamped, be drawn up for war’, in the uncontracted form -όωντο, with the final τ turned into θ before the rough breathing of ἱερά. Θήβης has the Ionic ending -ης. ῥα (= ἄρα) is ‘so, accordingly’; λίσσοντο ‘begged’ has the Mycenaeans as its unspoken object, and δόμεν is the epic infinitive of δίδωμι (= δοῦναι). κλειτούς is the same word as κλυτούς ‘famous’; ἐπίκουροι are ‘allies’.

sentences.t: οἳ δ’ ἔθελον δόμεναι καὶ ἐπῄνεον ὡς ἐκέλευον·
sentences.tr: hoi d’ ethelon domenai kai epēineon hōs ekeleuon·
sentences.l: And they were willing to give, and approved, as they were bidding;
sentences.i: and they were willing to give them, and gave their approval, as they bade.
sentences.n: Here οἳ δ’ switches to the Mycenaeans, who are asked. ἔθελον is without the augment (= ἤθελον), δόμεναι is an infinitive in -μεναι (= δοῦναι), and ἐπῄνεον ‘approved’ is the uncontracted form of ἐπῄνουν. ὡς ἐκέλευον ‘as they bade’ has the petitioners as its subject: the Mycenaeans agreed to what the Argives asked.

sentences.t: ἀλλὰ Ζεὺς ἔτρεψε παραίσια σήματα φαίνων.
sentences.tr: alla Zeus etrepse paraisia sēmata phainōn.
sentences.l: but Zeus turned them, showing unfitting signs.
sentences.i: But Zeus turned them from it, showing unfitting signs.
sentences.n: ἔτρεψε is the aorist of τρέπω ‘turn’, with the Mycenaeans understood as its object. παραίσια is an adjective built from παρά ‘beside, against’ and αἶσα ‘due portion’, so ‘not as it should be’; it is the opposite of ἐναίσιμος ‘fitting’, and means signs of ill omen. φαίνων is the present participle of φαίνω ‘show’.

sentences.t:
οἳ δ’ ἐπεὶ οὖν ᾤχοντο ἰδὲ πρὸ ὁδοῦ ἐγένοντο,
Ἀσωπὸν δ’ ἵκοντο βαθύσχοινον λεχεποίην,
ἔνθ’ αὖτ’ ἀγγελίην ἐπὶ Τυδῆ στεῖλαν Ἀχαιοί.
sentences.tr:
hoi d’ epei oun ōichonto ide pro hodou egenonto,
Asōpon d’ hikonto bathyschoinon lechepoiēn,
enth’ aut’ angeliēn epi Tydē steilan Achaioi.
sentences.l:
And when now they had gone off and got forward on the road,
and came to the Asopus, deep-rushed, grass-bedded,
there in turn an embassy upon Tydeus the Achaeans sent.
sentences.i: And when they had set out and were well on their way, they came to the Asopus, deep in rushes, with its beds of grass, and there in turn the Achaeans sent Tydeus on an embassy.
sentences.n: οἳ δ’ ‘and they’ are the Argives again. ᾤχοντο is from οἴχομαι ‘be gone, set off’; ἰδέ is the epic ‘and’; πρὸ ὁδοῦ ἐγένοντο ‘got forward on the road’ is an idiom. The δέ of Ἀσωπὸν δ’ ἵκοντο opens the main clause after the ἐπεί-clause. The Asopus is a river of Boeotia, with two epithets: βαθύσχοινον ‘deep in rushes’ (βαθύς ‘deep’ + σχοῖνος ‘rush’) and λεχεποίην ‘with its beds of grass’ (λέχος ‘bed’ + ποίη ‘grass’; a rare word, taken by the usual explanation). ἀγγελίη is ‘a message’, here the mission of an envoy, ‘an embassy’; Τυδῆ is the epic accusative of Τυδεύς, and ἐπί puts the errand on him. στεῖλαν = ἔστειλαν (no augment), from στέλλω ‘send’. Ἀχαιοί is the Argive army.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ὃ βῆ, πολέας δὲ κιχήσατο Καδμεΐωνας
δαινυμένους κατὰ δῶμα βίης Ἐτεοκληείης.
sentences.tr:
autar ho bē, poleas de kichēsato Kadmeïōnas
dainymenous kata dōma biēs Eteoklēeiēs.
sentences.l:
But he went, and many Cadmeans he came upon
feasting in the house of the might of Eteocles.
sentences.i: But he went on, and came upon many Cadmeans feasting in the house of the might of Eteocles.
sentences.n: ὃ ‘he’ is Tydeus, and βῆ is the aorist of βαίνω without the augment. πολέας is the epic form of πολλούς; κιχήσατο is the aorist middle of κιχάνω ‘come upon, find’. Καδμεΐωνες ‘Cadmeans’ are the Thebans, named for Cadmus, their founder. δαινυμένους is the participle of δαίνυμαι ‘feast’, and κατὰ δῶμα means ‘in the house’. βίης Ἐτεοκληείης ‘the might of Eteocles’ is a periphrasis for the man himself, the epic adjective Ἐτεοκληείης standing for a genitive, as in βίη Ἡρακληείη; it is Eteocles’ house where the Cadmeans feast.

sentences.t:
ἔνθ’ οὐδὲ ξεῖνός περ ἐὼν ἱππηλάτα Τυδεὺς
τάρβει, μοῦνος ἐὼν πολέσιν μετὰ Καδμείοισιν,
ἀλλ’ ὅ γ’ ἀεθλεύειν προκαλίζετο, πάντα δ’ ἐνίκα
ῥηϊδίως·
sentences.tr:
enth’ oude xeinos per eōn hippēlata Tydeus
tarbei, mounos eōn polesin meta Kadmeioisin,
all’ ho g’ aethleuein prokalizeto, panta d’ enika
rhēïdiōs·
sentences.l:
There not even though a stranger was horse-driver Tydeus
afraid, being alone among many Cadmeans,
but he kept challenging them to contend in contests, and everything he won
easily:
sentences.i: There Tydeus the horse-driver, stranger though he was, alone among many Cadmeans, was not afraid, but kept challenging them to compete in contests, and won at everything easily:
sentences.n: ἔνθ’ ‘there’; οὐδὲ … περ ἐών ‘not even though being’ is a concession, and ξεῖνος ‘stranger’ here stresses that he was a foreigner. ἱππηλάτα is the epic nominative (-α for -ης) of ἱππηλάτης ‘horse-driver’, a stock epithet. τάρβει is the imperfect of ταρβέω ‘be afraid’ without the augment. πολέσιν is epic for πολλοῖς, and Καδμείοισιν is the epic dative of Καδμεῖοι. ἀεθλεύειν ‘to contend in contests’ (the epic spelling of ἀθλεύειν) depends on προκαλίζετο, a middle imperfect, ‘kept challenging’. πάντα δ’ ἐνίκα ‘and he won everything’ runs on to ῥηϊδίως ‘easily’ at the start of the next line.

sentences.t: τοίη οἱ ἐπίρροθος ἦεν Ἀθήνη.
sentences.tr: toiē hoi epirrothos ēen Athēnē.
sentences.l: such a helper to him was Athena.
sentences.i: Such a helper was Athena to him.
sentences.n: τοίη ‘such’ points back: Athena’s help is the reason he won so easily. ἐπίρροθος is ‘helper’, a rare word; οἱ is the dative ‘to him’, and ἦεν = ἦν.

sentences.t:
οἳ δὲ χολωσάμενοι Καδμεῖοι κέντορες ἵππων
ἂψ ἄρ’ ἀνερχομένῳ πυκινὸν λόχον εἷσαν ἄγοντες
κούρους πεντήκοντα·
sentences.tr:
hoi de cholōsamenoi Kadmeioi kentores hippōn
aps ar’ anerchomenōi pykinon lochon heisan agontes
kourous pentēkonta·
sentences.i: But the enraged Cadmeans, goaders of horses, set a solid ambush against him as he was coming back, bringing fifty young men;
sentences.n: χολωσάμενοι is the aorist participle of χολόομαι ‘be enraged’, from χόλος ‘anger’. κέντορες ἵππων ‘goaders of horses’ is a stock epithet of the Cadmeans: κέντωρ comes from κεντέω ‘prick, goad’. ἂψ ‘back’ goes with ἀνερχομένῳ, a dative participle, ‘to him as he came back’. εἷσαν is an aorist of ἵζω ‘set, place’ (transitive), ‘they set’; πυκινόν ‘solid’ is the house word for πυκινός, here of a close-packed band. ἄγοντες ‘bringing’ and κούρους ‘young men’ name the ambushers themselves.

sentences.t:
δύω δ’ ἡγήτορες ἦσαν,
Μαίων Αἱμονίδης ἐπιείκελος ἀθανάτοισιν,
υἱός τ’ Αὐτοφόνοιο μενεπτόλεμος Πολυφόντης.
sentences.tr:
dyō d’ hēgētores ēsan,
Maiōn Haimonidēs epieikelos athanatoisin,
huios t’ Autophonoio meneptolemos Polyphontēs.
sentences.l:
and two leaders there were,
Maeon, Haemon’s-son, resembling the immortals,
and the son of Autophonus, steadfast-in-battle Polyphontes.
sentences.i: There were two leaders: Maeon, son of Haemon, who was like the immortals, and the son of Autophonus, Polyphontes, steadfast in battle.
sentences.n: δύω is ‘two’ (= δύο), and ἡγήτορες ‘leaders’ are the two who commanded the fifty. Αἱμονίδης is a patronymic in -ίδης, ‘son of Haemon’. ἐπιείκελος ἀθανάτοισιν ‘resembling the immortals’ is a stock phrase, with the dative of what he resembles. υἱός τ’ Αὐτοφόνοιο ‘and the son of Autophonus’ is Polyphontes, who is named last. μενεπτόλεμος ‘steadfast in battle’ is built from μένω ‘stay, stand firm’ and πτόλεμος, the epic form of πόλεμος ‘war’.

sentences.t: Τυδεὺς μὲν καὶ τοῖσιν ἀεικέα πότμον ἐφῆκε·
sentences.tr: Tydeus men kai toisin aeikea potmon ephēke·
sentences.l: Tydeus indeed upon these also an unseemly doom sent;
sentences.i: Tydeus sent an unseemly doom upon these men as well;
sentences.n: μέν looks forward to the δέ of the next line: ‘he killed them all, but one …’. καὶ τοῖσιν ‘upon these also’ (τοῖσιν is an epic dative plural of the pronoun). ἀεικέα πότμον ‘an unseemly doom’: πότμος is ‘lot, doom’, here death, and ἀεικής means ‘unseemly’. ἐφῆκε is the aorist of ἐφίημι ‘send upon, let loose on’.

sentences.t: πάντας ἔπεφν’, ἕνα δ’ οἶον ἵει οἶκον δὲ νέεσθαι·
sentences.tr: pantas epephn’, hena d’ oion hiei oikon de neesthai·
sentences.l: all he killed, but one alone he let go, home to return;
sentences.i: he killed them all, but let one man alone go back home;
sentences.n: ἔπεφν’ is the elided ἔπεφνε, an aorist of φένω ‘kill’ (the verb survives chiefly in the aorist). ἵει is the imperfect of ἵημι ‘let go, send’. οἶκον δέ ‘homeward’ is printed as two words in the edition, δέ being the suffix -δε of direction, and νέεσθαι ‘to return’ is the epic infinitive. The one man spared is named in the next line.

sentences.t: Μαίον’ ἄρα προέηκε θεῶν τεράεσσι πιθήσας.
sentences.tr: Maion’ ara proeēke theōn teraessi pithēsas.
sentences.l: Maeon, then, he sent forth, having obeyed the portents of the gods.
sentences.i: Maeon was the one he sent away, obeying the portents of the gods.
sentences.n: Μαίον’ is the elided accusative Μαίονα: he is the ‘one alone’ of the line before. προέηκε is the aorist of προΐημι ‘send forth’. τεράεσσι is the epic dative plural of τέρας ‘portent’, and πιθήσας is the aorist participle of πείθομαι ‘obey’, with the dative. Which portents these were is not said.

sentences.t: τοῖος ἔην Τυδεὺς Αἰτώλιος·
sentences.tr: toios eēn Tydeus Aitōlios·
sentences.l: Such was Tydeus the Aetolian;
sentences.i: Such a man was Tydeus the Aetolian;
sentences.n: τοῖος ἔην ‘such was’ closes the tale as τοίη did at 390; ἔην is the epic imperfect of εἰμί (= ἦν). Αἰτώλιος ‘Aetolian’ names Tydeus’ own country, Aetolia.

sentences.t:
ἀλλὰ τὸν υἱὸν
γείνατο εἷο χέρεια μάχῃ, ἀγορῇ δέ τ’ ἀμείνω.
sentences.tr:
alla ton huion
geinato heio chereia machēi, agorēi de t’ ameinō.
sentences.l:
but that son
he begot, than himself worse in fighting, but in assembly better.”
sentences.i: but the son he fathered is worse than himself in fighting, though better in assembly.”
sentences.n: τὸν υἱόν ‘that son’ is Diomedes, pointed out with the article. γείνατο is the aorist middle of γείνομαι, ‘beget’ when a father is the subject. εἷο is the epic genitive of the reflexive pronoun, ‘than himself’ (the genitive of comparison); χέρεια and ἀμείνω are accusatives (for χερείονα, ἀμείνονα), ‘worse’ and ‘better’, agreeing with υἱόν. μάχῃ ‘in fighting’ and ἀγορῇ ‘in assembly’ are datives of respect; ἀγορή is the meeting where men speak, so ‘better in assembly’ means better at speaking. Agamemnon’s speech ends here.

sentences.t:
ὣς φάτο, τὸν δ’ οὔ τι προσέφη κρατερὸς Διομήδης
αἰδεσθεὶς βασιλῆος ἐνιπὴν αἰδοίοιο·
sentences.tr:
hōs phato, ton d’ ou ti prosephē krateros Diomēdēs
aidestheis basilēos enipēn aidoioio·
sentences.l:
So he spoke, but him not at all addressed strong Diomedes,
having respected the rebuke of the revered king;
sentences.i: So he spoke, but strong Diomedes said nothing to him, respecting the rebuke of the revered king;
sentences.n: ὣς φάτο ‘so he spoke’ (φάτο is an aorist of φημί without the augment) closes the speech. τὸν δ’ οὔ τι προσέφη: προσέφη is ‘spoke to’, and οὔ τι ‘not at all’ makes it ‘said nothing to him’, which answers the μέν of 368. κρατερός ‘strong’ is a stock epithet of Diomedes. αἰδεσθείς is the aorist participle of αἰδέομαι ‘feel respect for’; ἐνιπή is ‘rebuke’, and αἰδοῖος ‘revered’ is the word for a person to whom respect is due. A new paragraph begins at 401.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ υἱὸς Καπανῆος ἀμείψατο κυδαλίμοιο·
sentences.tr: ton d’ huios Kapanēos ameipsato kydalimoio·
sentences.l: And him answered the son of glorious Capaneus:
sentences.i: Then the son of glorious Capaneus answered him:
sentences.n: ἀμείψατο is the aorist of ἀμείβομαι ‘answer’. The speaker is Sthenelus, but the poet does not name him: he is ‘the son of Capaneus’, with the epic genitive Καπανῆος (= Καπανέως) and its epithet κυδαλίμοιο ‘glorious’, a genitive in -οιο (= -ου).

sentences.t: Ἀτρεΐδη μὴ ψεύδε’ ἐπιστάμενος σάφα εἰπεῖν·
sentences.tr: Atreïdē mē pseude’ epistamenos sapha eipein·
sentences.l: “Atreus’-son, do not lie, knowing how to speak clearly:
sentences.i: “Son of Atreus, do not lie, when you know how to speak plainly;
sentences.n: Ἀτρεΐδη is the vocative of Ἀτρεΐδης ‘son of Atreus’. μὴ ψεύδε’ is a negative command: ψεύδε’ is the elided imperative ψεύδεο of ψεύδομαι ‘lie’. ἐπιστάμενος σάφα εἰπεῖν ‘knowing how to speak clearly’: ἐπίσταμαι with an infinitive means ‘know how to’, and σάφα is ‘clearly, accurately’. The charge is that the king knows better than what he has just said.

sentences.t: ἡμεῖς τοι πατέρων μέγ’ ἀμείνονες εὐχόμεθ’ εἶναι·
sentences.tr: hēmeis toi paterōn meg’ ameinones euchometh’ einai·
sentences.l: We indeed than our fathers much better claim to be;
sentences.i: We claim to be far better than our fathers;
sentences.n: ἡμεῖς ‘we’ is emphatic and is repeated at the start of the next line; τοι is a particle, ‘you see’ (originally σοι). πατέρων μέγ’ ἀμείνονες: the genitive of comparison ‘than fathers’, μέγα ‘by far’. εὐχόμεθ’ εἶναι ‘we claim to be’: εὔχομαι with an infinitive is ‘claim, boast’, not ‘pray’. The fathers are Tydeus and Capaneus.

sentences.t:
ἡμεῖς καὶ Θήβης ἕδος εἵλομεν ἑπταπύλοιο
παυρότερον λαὸν ἀγαγόνθ’ ὑπὸ τεῖχος ἄρειον,
πειθόμενοι τεράεσσι θεῶν καὶ Ζηνὸς ἀρωγῇ·
sentences.tr:
hēmeis kai Thēbēs hedos heilomen heptapyloio
pauroteron laon agagonth’ hypo teichos areion,
peithomenoi teraessi theōn kai Zēnos arōgēi·
sentences.i: We even took the seat of seven-gated Thebes, leading fewer troops under a stronger wall, obeying the portents of the gods and trusting in the help of Zeus;
sentences.n: ἡμεῖς καί ‘we even’. Θήβης ἕδος ‘the seat of Thebes’: ἕδος is ‘seat, base’, the place where a city sits, so here the city itself, and ἑπταπύλοιο ‘seven-gated’ is its stock epithet. εἵλομεν is the aorist of αἱρέω ‘take’. παυρότερον is the comparative of παῦρος ‘few’, ‘fewer’. ἀγαγόνθ’ is the aorist participle of ἄγω ‘lead’, its final τ turned θ before the rough breathing of ὑπό; whether it is a dual (‘we two leading’) or an elided plural is disputed. The line is metrically irregular as transmitted: the last syllable of λαόν, short by nature, has to stand in the long place of the third foot. τεῖχος ἄρειον ‘a stronger wall’: ἄρειον is a comparative of ἀγαθός, here ‘stronger’. πειθόμενοι ‘obeying’ takes the dative τεράεσσι ‘portents’ and, with Zeus’ ἀρωγῇ ‘help’, means ‘relying on’; Ζηνός = Διός.

sentences.t: κεῖνοι δὲ σφετέρῃσιν ἀτασθαλίῃσιν ὄλοντο·
sentences.tr: keinoi de spheterēisin atasthaliēisin olonto·
sentences.l: but those men, by their own wanton-follies, perished;
sentences.i: but they perished through their own wanton folly;
sentences.n: κεῖνοι is ἐκεῖνοι ‘those men’, the fathers. σφετέρῃσιν is the possessive ‘their own’ in the dative plural -ῃσιν; ἀτασθαλίαι ‘wanton follies’ is the house rendering (ἀτάσθαλος is ‘reckless, wicked’), and σφετέρῃσιν ἀτασθαλίῃσιν ὄλοντο is also a half-line of Odyssey 1.7. ὄλοντο is the aorist middle of ὄλλυμι ‘perish’, without the augment (= ὤλοντο).

sentences.t: τὼ μή μοι πατέρας ποθ’ ὁμοίῃ ἔνθεο τιμῇ.
sentences.tr: tō mē moi pateras poth’ homoiēi entheo timēi.
sentences.l: Therefore not for me our fathers ever in like honour put.”
sentences.i: So do not ever place our fathers in the same honour as us.”
sentences.n: τώ (= τῷ) is ‘therefore’. μή μοι: μοι is a dative of the person concerned, ‘I ask’, and the negative command is ἔνθεο, the aorist imperative middle of ἐντίθημι ‘put in’; ποθ’ = ποτε ‘ever’. ὁμοίῃ τιμῇ ‘in like honour’ is the dative of the place the fathers are not to be put in; the honour paid to the speakers is understood as the thing compared. Sthenelus’ speech ends here.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἄρ’ ὑπόδρα ἰδὼν προσέφη κρατερὸς Διομήδης·
sentences.tr: ton d’ ar’ hypodra idōn prosephē krateros Diomēdēs·
sentences.l: Him then with a scowl looking addressed strong Diomedes:
sentences.i: Then strong Diomedes, looking at him with a scowl, spoke to him:
sentences.n: This is the formula for an answer given with a dark look; the Odyssey has it for Odysseus at 8.165. ὑπόδρα is an adverb, ‘from under (the brows)’, ‘with a scowl’; its derivation is not certain. ἰδών ‘looking’, προσέφη ‘addressed’, κρατερός ‘strong’. A new paragraph begins at 411.

sentences.t: τέττα, σιωπῇ ἧσο, ἐμῷ δ’ ἐπιπείθεο μύθῳ·
sentences.tr: tetta, siōpēi hēso, emōi d’ epipeitheo mythōi·
sentences.l: “Friend, in silence sit, and obey my word;
sentences.i: “Friend, sit in silence, and obey my word;
sentences.n: τέττα is a word of familiar address whose origin and exact force are not known; ‘friend’ is the sense the context gives. σιωπῇ ‘in silence’ is a dative, and ἧσο is the imperative of ἧμαι ‘sit’. ἐπιπείθεο is the imperative middle of ἐπιπείθομαι ‘obey’, with the dative ἐμῷ μύθῳ ‘my word’; the ending -εο is the epic form of -ου.

sentences.t:
οὐ γὰρ ἐγὼ νεμεσῶ Ἀγαμέμνονι ποιμένι λαῶν
ὀτρύνοντι μάχεσθαι ἐϋκνήμιδας Ἀχαιούς·
sentences.tr:
ou gar egō nemesō Agamemnoni poimeni laōn
otrynonti machesthai eÿknēmidas Achaious·
sentences.l:
For I do not feel resentment at Agamemnon, shepherd of the people,
urging the well-greaved Achaeans to fight;
sentences.i: For I feel no resentment at Agamemnon, shepherd of the people, when he urges the well-greaved Achaeans to fight;
sentences.n: νεμεσῶ is from νεμεσάω ‘feel resentment’, which takes the dative of the person, here Agamemnon. ποιμένι λαῶν ‘shepherd of the people’ is a stock epithet of kings. ὀτρύνοντι is a dative participle, ‘as he urges’ (ὀτρύνω ‘urge on’), and μάχεσθαι ‘to fight’ says what he urges. ἐϋκνήμιδας Ἀχαιούς ‘well-greaved Achaeans’ is the stock phrase, with the diaeresis printed. Diomedes does not resent the rebuke: it is the king’s part to urge the army on.

sentences.t:
τούτῳ μὲν γὰρ κῦδος ἅμ’ ἕψεται εἴ κεν Ἀχαιοὶ
Τρῶας δῃώσωσιν ἕλωσί τε Ἴλιον ἱρήν,
τούτῳ δ’ αὖ μέγα πένθος Ἀχαιῶν δῃωθέντων.
sentences.tr:
toutōi men gar kydos ham’ hepsetai ei ken Achaioi
Trōas dēiōsōsin helōsi te Ilion hirēn,
toutōi d’ au mega penthos Achaiōn dēiōthentōn.
sentences.l:
For to this man glory will go along, if the Achaeans
cut down the Trojans and take sacred Ilium,
and to this man in turn great grief, the Achaeans having been cut down.
sentences.i: For glory will attend him if the Achaeans cut down the Trojans and take sacred Ilium, and on the other hand great grief will be his if the Achaeans are cut down.
sentences.n: τούτῳ ‘to this man’ is Agamemnon, repeated for the contrast μέν … δ’ αὖ ‘on the one hand … on the other’. ἅμ’ ἕψεται ‘will go along with’ is a future of ἕπομαι. εἴ κεν with the aorist subjunctives δῃώσωσιν and ἕλωσι looks forward: ‘if (as may happen) they …’. δῃόω is ‘cut down’, of men in battle; ἱρήν = ἱερήν ‘sacred’, the stock epithet of Ilium. The last clause has no verb (‘there will be’ is understood), and the genitive absolute Ἀχαιῶν δῃωθέντων ‘the Achaeans having been cut down’ gives its condition.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ ἄγε δὴ καὶ νῶϊ μεδώμεθα θούριδος ἀλκῆς.
sentences.tr: all’ age dē kai nōï medōmetha thouridos alkēs.
sentences.l: But come now, let us two also be mindful of impetuous might.”
sentences.i: But come, let us two also be mindful of impetuous might.”
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ἄγε δή ‘but come now’ rouses to action. νῶϊ is the dual pronoun ‘we two’ (Diomedes and Sthenelus), and μεδώμεθα is a subjunctive of exhortation, ‘let us’, from μέδομαι ‘be mindful of’, which takes the genitive θούριδος ἀλκῆς. θοῦρις is ‘rushing, impetuous’ and ἀλκή is ‘might’. Diomedes’ speech ends here.

sentences.t: ἦ ῥα καὶ ἐξ ὀχέων σὺν τεύχεσιν ἆλτο χαμᾶζε·
sentences.tr: ē rha kai ex ocheōn syn teuchesin alto chamaze·
sentences.l: He spoke, and from the chariot with his armour leapt to the ground;
sentences.i: So he said, and leapt from the chariot to the ground with his armour;
sentences.n: ἦ ῥα καί ‘so he said, and’: ἦ is the old ‘he said’, ῥα (= ἄρα) a particle; the phrase closes the speech and starts the action. ὀχέων is the plural of ὄχος ‘chariot’, which often stands for one vehicle, and ἐξ ὀχέων is ‘out of the chariot’. τεύχεσιν with σύν is ‘with his armour’. ἆλτο is the aorist middle of ἅλλομαι ‘leap’ without the augment, and χαμᾶζε ‘to the ground’ has the suffix -ζε of direction, like -δε. A new paragraph begins at 419.

sentences.t:
δεινὸν δ’ ἔβραχε χαλκὸς ἐπὶ στήθεσσιν ἄνακτος
ὀρνυμένου·
sentences.tr:
deinon d’ ebrache chalkos epi stēthessin anaktos
ornymenou·
sentences.l:
and fearsomely clanged the bronze upon the chest of the lord
as he sprang;
sentences.i: The bronze clanged fearsomely on the chest of the lord as he sprang;
sentences.n: δεινόν is an adverb here, ‘fearsomely’. ἔβραχε is an aorist of βράχω ‘clang, crash’; the bronze is his armour. στήθεσσιν is the epic dative plural of στῆθος ‘chest’. ἄνακτος ‘of the lord’ is Diomedes, and ὀρνυμένου, a genitive participle of ὄρνυμαι ‘spring, rush’, agrees with it.

sentences.t: ὑπό κεν ταλασίφρονά περ δέος εἷλεν.
sentences.tr: hypo ken talasiphrona per deos heilen.
sentences.l: from under would even an enduring-minded man fear have taken.
sentences.i: fear would have taken hold of even a steadfast man.
sentences.n: ὑπό … εἷλεν is tmesis: the preverb ὑπό stands apart from the verb, ‘take from under’, that is, seize. κεν with the aorist εἷλεν makes it ‘would have taken’. ταλασίφρονα is the accusative of ταλασίφρων ‘enduring-minded’ (‘steadfast’ in the free translation), and περ ‘even’ makes the point: even the steadiest man would have been afraid. δέος is ‘fear’.

sentences.t:
ὡς δ’ ὅτ’ ἐν αἰγιαλῷ πολυηχέϊ κῦμα θαλάσσης
ὄρνυτ’ ἐπασσύτερον Ζεφύρου ὕπο κινήσαντος·
sentences.tr:
hōs d’ hot’ en aigialōi polyēcheï kyma thalassēs
ornyt’ epassyteron Zephyrou hypo kinēsantos·
sentences.l:
And as when on the much-resounding beach a wave of the sea
rises, one close upon another, by the West Wind having stirred it;
sentences.i: As when a wave of the sea rises on a loud-resounding beach, one close upon another, when the West Wind has stirred it;
sentences.n: ὡς δ’ ὅτε ‘and as when’ opens a simile, and ὣς τότε at 427 returns to the army. αἰγιαλός is a beach; πολυηχέϊ is the dative of πολυηχής ‘much-resounding’ (πολύς and ἠχή ‘sound’). ὄρνυτ’ is ὄρνυτο, a past tense used in a simile for what always happens, and ἐπασσύτερον ‘one close upon another’ is an adverb. Ζεφύρου ὕπο κινήσαντος is a genitive absolute, ‘the West Wind having stirred it’, with ὕπο ‘from below’ standing beside the participle as an adverb. A new paragraph begins at 422.

sentences.t:
πόντῳ μέν τε πρῶτα κορύσσεται, αὐτὰρ ἔπειτα
χέρσῳ ῥηγνύμενον μεγάλα βρέμει, ἀμφὶ δέ τ’ ἄκρας
κυρτὸν ἐὸν κορυφοῦται, ἀποπτύει δ’ ἁλὸς ἄχνην·
sentences.tr:
pontōi men te prōta koryssetai, autar epeita
chersōi rhēgnymenon megala bremei, amphi de t’ akras
kyrton eon koryphoutai, apoptyei d’ halos achnēn·
sentences.i: On the open sea it first arms itself, but then, breaking on dry land, it roars loudly, and around the capes, arching, it rises to a peak and spits out the spray of the sea;
sentences.n: μέν τε … αὐτὰρ ἔπειτα ‘at first … but then’; τε is the epic particle of a general statement. κορύσσεται is the middle of κορύσσω ‘arm oneself’, from κόρυς ‘helmet’: the wave puts on a helmet when its crest forms (the verb returns for Strife at 442). χέρσῳ is the dative of χέρσος ‘dry land’; ῥηγνύμενον ‘breaking’; βρέμει ‘roars’. ἄκρας ‘capes’ is from ἄκρα, a headland, and κυρτὸν ἐόν is ‘being arched’ (ἐόν = ὄν). κορυφοῦται ‘rises to a peak’ comes from κορυφή ‘peak’, ἀποπτύει is ‘spits out’, and ἁλός is the genitive of ἅλς ‘sea’, with ἄχνην ‘spray’.

sentences.t:
ὣς τότ’ ἐπασσύτεραι Δαναῶν κίνυντο φάλαγγες
νωλεμέως πόλεμον δέ·
sentences.tr:
hōs tot’ epassyterai Danaōn kinynto phalanges
nōlemeōs polemon de·
sentences.l:
So then, one close upon another, moved the battle-lines of the Danaans
unceasingly to war;
sentences.i: So then the battle-lines of the Danaans moved, one close upon another, without pause toward war;
sentences.n: ὣς τότε answers the simile: ‘so then’. ἐπασσύτεραι is the feminine plural of the adjective, whose neuter is the adverb used of the wave at 423, and names the point of likeness: line after line. κίνυντο is the imperfect of κίνυμαι ‘move’, φάλαγγες are ‘battle-lines’, and Δαναῶν is the genitive of Δαναοί, here the whole army. νωλεμέως is ‘unceasingly’; πόλεμον δέ ‘to war’ is two words in the edition, with the suffix -δε of direction.

sentences.t:
κέλευε δὲ οἷσιν ἕκαστος
ἡγεμόνων·
sentences.tr:
keleue de hoisin hekastos
hēgemonōn·
sentences.l:
and was bidding his own men each
of the leaders;
sentences.i: and each of the leaders gave orders to his own men;
sentences.n: κέλευε is the imperfect of κελεύω ‘bid, order’ without the augment. οἷσιν is the possessive ὅς ‘his own’ in the dative plural, with its noun ‘men’ left out, and ἕκαστος ἡγεμόνων ‘each of the leaders’ is the subject: each leader orders his own men.

sentences.t:
οἳ δ’ ἄλλοι ἀκὴν ἴσαν, οὐδέ κε φαίης
τόσσον λαὸν ἕπεσθαι ἔχοντ’ ἐν στήθεσιν αὐδήν,
σιγῇ δειδιότες σημάντορας·
sentences.tr:
hoi d’ alloi akēn isan, oude ke phaiēs
tosson laon hepesthai echont’ en stēthesin audēn,
sigēi deidiotes sēmantoras·
sentences.i: while the rest went on hushed; you would not have said that so many troops followed with a voice in their breasts, in silence, fearing those who gave the orders;
sentences.n: οἳ δ’ ἄλλοι ‘while the others’ are the rank and file. ἀκήν is an adverb, ‘hushed’, and ἴσαν, from εἶμι, is ‘they went’. οὐδέ κε φαίης is a potential optative of the second person, ‘nor would you say’, that is, any onlooker. τόσσον λαόν is singular, ‘so great a people’, while the participle δειδιότες ‘fearing’ (perfect of δείδω) is plural, agreeing in sense. ἔχοντ’ ἐν στήθεσιν αὐδήν ‘having a voice in their chests’: no one could have told that they could speak. σημάντορας ‘those who give the orders’, from σημαίνω ‘give orders’, is a rare word.

sentences.t:
ἀμφὶ δὲ πᾶσι
τεύχεα ποικίλ’ ἔλαμπε, τὰ εἱμένοι ἐστιχόωντο.
sentences.tr:
amphi de pasi
teuchea poikil’ elampe, ta heimenoi estichoōnto.
sentences.l:
and around all
the intricate armour shone, which clothed in they were marching.
sentences.i: and about all of them shone the intricate armour that they wore as they marched.
sentences.n: ἀμφὶ … πᾶσι ‘around them all’. τεύχεα ποικίλ’ is ‘intricate armour’ (ποικίλος ‘intricate’, of worked surfaces), and ἔλαμπε is ‘shone’. τά is the relative ‘which’; εἱμένοι is the perfect passive participle of ἕννυμι ‘clothe’, ‘clothed in’, with τά as what they wear. ἐστιχόωντο is the uncontracted imperfect of στιχάομαι ‘march in line’, from στίχες ‘ranks’.

sentences.t:
Τρῶες δ’, ὥς τ’ ὄϊες πολυπάμονος ἀνδρὸς ἐν αὐλῇ
μυρίαι ἑστήκασιν ἀμελγόμεναι γάλα λευκὸν
ἀζηχὲς μεμακυῖαι ἀκούουσαι ὄπα ἀρνῶν,
ὣς Τρώων ἀλαλητὸς ἀνὰ στρατὸν εὐρὺν ὀρώρει·
sentences.tr:
Trōes d’, hōs t’ oïes polypamonos andros en aulēi
myriai hestēkasin amelgomenai gala leukon
azēches memakuiai akouousai opa arnōn,
hōs Trōōn alalētos ana straton euryn orōrei·
sentences.l:
And the Trojans — as sheep of a man of many possessions in the courtyard,
countless, stand being milked of white milk,
incessantly bleating, hearing the voice of their lambs,
so of the Trojans the outcry through the wide army had sprung up;
sentences.i: As for the Trojans — like countless sheep of a man of many possessions, standing in his courtyard to be milked of their white milk, bleating incessantly as they hear the voice of their lambs — so the outcry of the Trojans went up through the wide army;
sentences.n: Τρῶες δ’ begins a sentence that changes shape after the simile: it is picked up as a genitive, ὣς Τρώων … ‘so of the Trojans …’. ὥς τε opens the comparison. ὄϊες is the plural of ὄϊς ‘sheep’ (= οἶς). πολυπάμων ‘of many possessions’ is usually derived from πᾶμα ‘possession’, but the formation is not certain. μυρίαι ‘countless’; ἑστήκασιν ‘stand’, a perfect with present sense; ἀμελγόμεναι ‘being milked’, from ἀμέλγω; ἀζηχές ‘incessantly’, an adverb; μεμακυῖαι, the feminine perfect participle of μηκάομαι ‘bleat’; ὄπα, accusative of ὄψ ‘voice’. ἀλαλητός is a shout (ἀλαλά was a battle-cry), and ὀρώρει is the pluperfect of ὄρνυμι, ‘had risen’.

sentences.t:
οὐ γὰρ πάντων ἦεν ὁμὸς θρόος οὐδ’ ἴα γῆρυς,
ἀλλὰ γλῶσσα μέμικτο, πολύκλητοι δ’ ἔσαν ἄνδρες.
sentences.tr:
ou gar pantōn ēen homos throos oud’ ia gērys,
alla glōssa memikto, polyklētoi d’ esan andres.
sentences.l:
For of all there was not the same sound, nor one voice,
but their tongue was mixed, and many-summoned were the men.
sentences.i: For they did not all have the same sound, or one voice, but their tongue was mixed, and the men were summoned from many places.
sentences.n: οὐ γάρ … explains why the Trojan noise is like bleating: there was no one speech. ἦεν = ἦν. ὁμὸς θρόος ‘the same sound’ and ἴα γῆρυς ‘one voice’ say much the same thing twice; ἴα is Ionic for μία ‘one’. μέμικτο is the pluperfect passive of μίγνυμι ‘mix’, and γλῶσσα ‘tongue’ here means language. πολύκλητοι, from πολύς and καλέω ‘call’, means ‘called from many places’, as allies are; ἔσαν = ἦσαν.

sentences.t:
ὄρσε δὲ τοὺς μὲν Ἄρης, τοὺς δὲ γλαυκῶπις Ἀθήνη
Δεῖμός τ’ ἠδὲ Φόβος καὶ Ἔρις ἄμοτον μεμαυῖα,
Ἄρεος ἀνδροφόνοιο κασιγνήτη ἑτάρη τε,
sentences.tr:
orse de tous men Arēs, tous de glaukōpis Athēnē
Deimos t’ ēde Phobos kai Eris amoton memauia,
Areos androphonoio kasignētē hetarē te,
sentences.l:
And roused these Ares, and those gleaming-eyed Athena,
and Dread and Terror and Strife, unceasingly eager,
of man-slaying Ares the sister and companion,
sentences.i: Ares roused the one side and gleaming-eyed Athena the other, and Dread and Terror and Strife, eager without ceasing, the sister and companion of man-slaying Ares,
sentences.n: ὄρσε is the aorist of ὄρνυμι ‘rouse’ without the augment; it is singular, agreeing with Ares, the first subject, though the others are added after it. τοὺς μέν … τοὺς δέ ‘these … those’ divide the two armies, but the Greek does not say which god roused which. γλαυκῶπις ‘gleaming-eyed’ is Athena’s stock epithet. Δεῖμος and Φόβος are dread and terror as persons, and Ἔρις is strife as a person, so the English capitalises them. ἄμοτον μεμαυῖα: μεμαυῖα is the feminine perfect participle of μέμονα ‘be eager’, and the sense of ἄμοτον is not known (‘unceasingly’ is the traditional guess). ἀνδροφόνος ‘man-slaying’ is Ares’ stock epithet, and ἑτάρη is the feminine of ἑταῖρος ‘companion’.

sentences.t:
ἥ τ’ ὀλίγη μὲν πρῶτα κορύσσεται, αὐτὰρ ἔπειτα
οὐρανῷ ἐστήριξε κάρη καὶ ἐπὶ χθονὶ βαίνει·
sentences.tr:
hē t’ oligē men prōta koryssetai, autar epeita
ouranōi estērixe karē kai epi chthoni bainei·
sentences.l:
who small at first arms herself, but then
in heaven plants her head and on the earth walks;
sentences.i: who is small when she first arms herself, but then she plants her head in heaven and walks upon the earth;
sentences.n: ἥ τε ‘who’ (the epic τε marks a general truth about Strife). ὀλίγη ‘small’ describes her as she is at first. κορύσσεται repeats the verb used of the wave at 424, here ‘arms herself’, with the sense of rearing up. ἐστήριξε is a gnomic aorist, a past form that states what always happens, ‘plants’; οὐρανῷ is the dative of place, ‘in heaven’; κάρη is the accusative ‘head’; βαίνει is ‘walks’.

sentences.t:
ἥ σφιν καὶ τότε νεῖκος ὁμοίϊον ἔμβαλε μέσσῳ
ἐρχομένη καθ’ ὅμιλον ὀφέλλουσα στόνον ἀνδρῶν.
sentences.tr:
hē sphin kai tote neikos homoiïon embale messōi
erchomenē kath’ homilon ophellousa stonon andrōn.
sentences.l:
She to them even then a quarrel common to all threw into the midst
going through the throng, increasing the groaning of men.
sentences.i: She it was who then too threw a quarrel, the same for all, into the midst of them as she went through the throng, increasing the groaning of men.
sentences.n: ἥ here is the pronoun ‘she’, Strife, not the relative of the line before. σφιν is the dative ‘to them, among them’; καὶ τότε ‘even then’; ἔμβαλε ‘threw in’ takes μέσσῳ ‘into the midst’. ὁμοίϊον means ‘alike, common to all’: the usual explanation is that the strife was the same for both sides, but how it is meant is not certain. ὀφέλλουσα ‘increasing’ is from ὀφέλλω.

sentences.t:
οἳ δ’ ὅτε δή ῥ’ ἐς χῶρον ἕνα ξυνιόντες ἵκοντο,
σύν ῥ’ ἔβαλον ῥινούς, σὺν δ’ ἔγχεα καὶ μένε’ ἀνδρῶν
χαλκεοθωρήκων·
sentences.tr:
hoi d’ hote dē rh’ es chōron hena xyniontes hikonto,
syn rh’ ebalon rhinous, syn d’ enchea kai mene’ andrōn
chalkeothōrēkōn·
sentences.i: And when they had come together into one place, they dashed together their hide shields, their spears, and the might of men in bronze breastplates;
sentences.n: οἳ δ’ ὅτε δή ῥ’ ‘and when indeed’ (ῥα = ἄρα) opens the clash. ξυνιόντες is the participle of ξύνειμι ‘come together’, and ἵκοντο is the aorist ‘reached’. σὺν … ἔβαλον is tmesis of συμβάλλω ‘dash together’, and σύν is repeated before ἔγχεα. ῥινούς are ‘hides’, that is, shields covered with hide; μένε’ is the elided plural of μένος ‘might’. χαλκεοθωρήκων ‘in bronze breastplates’ is a compound of χάλκεος ‘bronze’ and θώρηξ ‘breastplate’. A new paragraph begins at 446.

sentences.t:
ἀτὰρ ἀσπίδες ὀμφαλόεσσαι
ἔπληντ’ ἀλλήλῃσι, πολὺς δ’ ὀρυμαγδὸς ὀρώρει.
sentences.tr:
atar aspides omphaloessai
eplēnt’ allēlēisi, polys d’ orymagdos orōrei.
sentences.l:
and the bossed shields
were brought together with one another, and a great din had sprung up.
sentences.i: and the bossed shields clashed together, and a great din went up.
sentences.n: ἀτάρ is ‘and, but’. ὀμφαλόεσσαι ‘bossed’ describes shields with an ὀμφαλός, the central boss. ἔπληντ’ is the elided aorist ἔπληντο of πελάζω ‘bring near’, here passive, ‘were brought up against’ one another (ἀλλήλῃσι, a dative). The half-line πολὺς δ’ ὀρυμαγδὸς ὀρώρει also ends 2.810.

sentences.t:
ἔνθα δ’ ἅμ’ οἰμωγή τε καὶ εὐχωλὴ πέλεν ἀνδρῶν
ὀλλύντων τε καὶ ὀλλυμένων, ῥέε δ’ αἵματι γαῖα.
sentences.tr:
entha d’ ham’ oimōgē te kai euchōlē pelen andrōn
ollyntōn te kai ollymenōn, rhee d’ haimati gaia.
sentences.l:
There together were wailing and boasting of men
destroying and perishing, and flowed with blood the earth.
sentences.i: There together were the wailing and the boasting of men killing and being killed, and the earth ran with blood.
sentences.n: ἔνθα δ’ ‘there’. ἅμ’ ‘together, at once’ goes with the pair οἰμωγή τε καὶ εὐχωλή: a cry of pain and a victor’s boast. πέλεν is the imperfect of πέλομαι ‘be, come to be’, without the augment. ἀνδρῶν is shared by both nouns and by the two participles ὀλλύντων and ὀλλυμένων, active ‘killing’ and passive ‘being killed’, from ὄλλυμι. ῥέε δ’ αἵματι γαῖα: αἵματι is a dative of means, ‘ran with blood’.

sentences.t:
ὡς δ’ ὅτε χείμαρροι ποταμοὶ κατ’ ὄρεσφι ῥέοντες
ἐς μισγάγκειαν συμβάλλετον ὄβριμον ὕδωρ
κρουνῶν ἐκ μεγάλων κοίλης ἔντοσθε χαράδρης,
τῶν δέ τε τηλόσε δοῦπον ἐν οὔρεσιν ἔκλυε ποιμήν·
sentences.tr:
hōs d’ hote cheimarroi potamoi kat’ oresphi rheontes
es misgankeian symballeton obrimon hydōr
krounōn ek megalōn koilēs entosthe charadrēs,
tōn de te tēlose doupon en ouresin eklye poimēn·
sentences.i: As when two winter torrents, rivers flowing down the mountains, pour their mighty water together where the glens meet, from great springs, inside a hollow ravine, and far off in the mountains a shepherd hears the crash of them;
sentences.n: ὡς δ’ ὅτε opens a third simile, after the wave at 422 and the ewes at 433. χείμαρροι is ‘winter-flowing’ (χεῖμα ‘winter’ + ῥέω ‘flow’): streams swollen in the rainy season. κατ’ ὄρεσφι is ‘down the mountains’, with the suffix -φι. συμβάλλετον is a dual verb, ‘the two throw together’: two torrents meet, though ποταμοί is plural. μισγάγκεια is ‘the place where glens meet’ (μίσγω ‘mix’ + ἄγκος ‘glen’); κρουνῶν are ‘springs’; κοίλης … χαράδρης is ‘a hollow ravine’, with ἔντοσθε ‘inside’ taking the genitive. τηλόσε ‘far off’ has the suffix -σε of direction, δοῦπον is ‘crash’, and ἔκλυε is an aorist stating what always happens, ‘hears’.

sentences.t: ὣς τῶν μισγομένων γένετο ἰαχή τε πόνος τε.
sentences.tr: hōs tōn misgomenōn geneto iachē te ponos te.
sentences.l: So of them mingling arose a cry and toil.
sentences.i: So as they mingled together, a cry and toil arose.
sentences.n: ὣς closes the simile and turns it back to the armies. τῶν μισγομένων is a genitive absolute, ‘as they mingled’: the participle is from μίσγω, the verb inside μισγάγκεια, so the meeting of the torrents and the meeting of the armies are one image. γένετο is the aorist of γίγνομαι without the augment, ‘arose’; ἰαχή is a shout, and πόνος is the toil of fighting. The part ends here, in the middle of the battle.
